extracted.intended_audience: students, researchers, and practitioners in literary studies, rhetoric, composition, and genre theory
extracted.subtask_description: Overview of conceptual criteria and analytic dimensions from genre studies for analyzing, classifying, or producing texts across social and historical contexts. Emphasizes rhetorical situations, social construction, activity systems, and tensions between stability and change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Written (textual) genres are social constructions
rubrics_metrics.description: "Written (textual) genres are social constructions that represent specific purposes for reading and writing within different social activities, created by social groups who need them to perform certain things. They change over time, reflecting essential shifts in social function performed by that text. Genres also represent constellations of textual attributes: some attributes are necessary and other attributes are optional.",
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this as a diagnostic: identify the social activity a text serves, which attributes are treated as necessary vs optional in that community, and trace historical change in those functions. Remember genres are created by social groups to accomplish purposes rather than being fixed natural kinds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genres as 'typified rhetorical actions' (Miller)
rubrics_metrics.description: Genres are "typified rhetorical actions" that respond to recurring situations and become instantiated in groups' behaviors; genre should be "centered not on the substance or the form of discourse but on the action it is used to accomplish."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate texts by the recurrent situation they respond to and the social action they perform. To theorize change, track how 'types' (recognition of relevant similarities) evolve as past routines are adapted into new routines to produce new types.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rhetorical situation (Bitzer) — exigence, audience, constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: Bitzer describes rhetorical situations as containing three components: exigence, audience, and constraints; he highlights six characteristics: a situation calls discourse into existence; it invites a response to fit the situation; the response meets necessary requirements of the situation; the exigence is located in reality; rhetorical situations exhibit simple or complex structures; and rhetorical situations after creation either decline or persist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing or composing, identify the concrete exigence, the relevant audience, and constraints shaping allowable responses. Assess whether a proposed rhetorical move fits situational requirements and whether the situation is likely to persist or resolve.

rubrics_metrics.name: Antecedent genres as rhetorical constraints (Jamieson)
rubrics_metrics.description: Antecedent genres are genres of the past that are used as a basis to shape and form current rhetorical responses; they can impose powerful constraints and may cause rhetors to become "bound by the manacles of the antecedent genre."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check when writers draw on historical/precedent genres and whether those antecedents are appropriate; be cautious that reliance on antecedents can produce mismatches with current situational demands and limit innovation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reciprocity of genre (Devitt)
rubrics_metrics.description: A genre is named because of its formal markers, and "the formal markers can be defined because a genre has been named" — genre and situation are reciprocals: naming signals formal markers which in turn define recognition of the genre.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In practice, examine how labeling a text shapes expectations and how recurring situational features both produce and are produced by genre labels. Use examples (e.g., grocery lists) to show how naming and recognition co-construct genre boundaries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tyranny of genre — constraints on creativity and reception
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'tyranny of genre' signifies how generic structures constrain individual creativity: the presence of conventional features yields strong genre identification, fewer features or mixing features yields weak or ambiguous identification; genres also create a "horizon of expectation" guiding reader interpretation and can polarize responses to mixed-genre texts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this to explain reader resistance to hybrid works and to evaluate risks when combining conventions. Consider pedagogical or editorial implications: whether to privilege genre conformity or encourage modification of genres.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stabilization, homogenization, and fixity
rubrics_metrics.description: Stabilization refers to degrees of predictable discourse within a genre; homogenization concerns similarity across instances; fixity is deliberately utilized prior to rhetorical situations and affects stabilization. Choice of a fixed arena can alter homogenization and lead to new or modernized micro-genres.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess how fixed conventions are within a genre, where variability occurs, and whether actors deliberately invoke fixity. Track how choices about fixity and homogenization produce stability or open space for genre innovation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genre ecology and activity theory (genres as mediating tools)
rubrics_metrics.description: Activity theory models how multiple factors (subject, object, mediating artifacts, rules, division of labor) in an activity system interact. "Genre ecology" describes dense connections between genres within the activities they mediate: multiple genres mediate a single activity; no genre exists in isolation. Genres are "tools-in-use" and mediating objects within an activity system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze texts not in isolation but as part of an ecology of genres mediating an activity system (e.g., organizational communication). Identify related genres, roles, tools, rules, and how changes (like digitization) reconfigure genre forms and distributions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Texts as objects or tools; user grounding and uptake (Geisler, Swarts)
rubrics_metrics.description: Texts may function as mediational means to complete a task or be valued as objects (outcomes) in discourse communities. Users 'ground' texts by altering structure for personal use, transforming a 'formalized representation of information' into a personal tool; meaning is established by uptake of users.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating a text's design or usability, determine whether it is intended as a tool or an object, and observe how end-users adapt and repurpose it. Investigate uptake practices to understand how genre meanings are negotiated in use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary vs secondary speech genres (Bakhtin)
rubrics_metrics.description: Primary speech genres are short, quotidian utterances (rejoinders, everyday narration, commands, letters, diaries); complex secondary speech genres (novels, dramas, scientific research) arise by absorbing and altering primary genres, undergoing dialogization and then finalization into a semantically exhaustive whole prepared for responsive understanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this distinction to trace how everyday communicative moves are transformed within large-scale texts; examine processes of absorption, dialogization, and finalization to see how genres incorporate multiple voices and conventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genres enact community identities and legitimate practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Rhetorical moves people must make within accepted genres to communicate successfully in particular contexts operate to reinforce communities' identities and to legitimate particular communication practices; genres structure members' ways of creating, interpreting, and using knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate how adherence to or deviation from genre conventions affects community membership, authority, and knowledge production. Consider pedagogical strategies to teach genre moves that enact disciplinary identities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits and problems of genre classification (overlap, loss of individual merit)
rubrics_metrics.description: Genre has limitations: classification is difficult because information overlaps and single works can encompass multiple genres; when classification is used to assign value judgments, preconceptions about the whole can influence opinion of the individual and the merit of the individual may be lost.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious using genre labels as evaluative shortcuts. In criticism or editorial decisions, weigh a work's unique qualities alongside its generic affiliations and avoid rigid value judgments based solely on genre classification.
